newsitem.title: USA: US crude outlook-pegged on heat, resistance ahead.
newsitem.headline: US crude outlook-pegged on heat, resistance ahead.

text.p: U.S. crude prices are looking somewhat defensive devoid of supply shortages and with autumn refinery turnarounds likely to take a bite out of demand, traders and analysts said on Monday.
But limited imports and high refinery runs for the moment seem to have stalled the crude price erosion, with bullish heating oil also acting as a price prop.
"There is no pressure anywhere on crude supplies. It will probably continue to trade in a range on low volume, and be products-related," an East Coast cash trader said.
U.S. refiners have delayed purchases of November crude, relying on domestic grades while foreign cargoes have been out of reach due to the narrow arbitrage.
With North Sea refiners buying furiously last week, and removing a chunk of supplies, domestic grades ought to find support while U.S. refiners catch up on requirements.
NYMEX November crude reached an intraday high of $24.80 a barrel early Monday, after setting a contract high last week at $24.62 a barrel.
The range this week is expected to be between near-term support at $23.80 a barrel, and resistance at $24.60 a barrel.
While acknowleding crude's overbought condition, traders were not willing to bet against the market matching five-year and post-Gulf War highs at $25.70 a barrel in the mid-term.
MidEast tensions sparked by Palestinian-Israeli violence recently, and uncertainties over Russia's oil exports could add sporadic upward momentum, traders said.
"MidEast tensions won't have much bearing short-term, but Russian uncertainties have given people more jitters," Cyrus Tahmassebi, president of Energy Trends Inc. said.
Concerns about Russian President Boris Yeltsin's heart surgery was supportive in the absence of bullish fundamentals.
Bill O'Grady, energy analyst for A.G. Edwards & Sons in St. Louis, said he expected the energy complex to move higher however on the strength in seasonal products fundamentals.
"There is a little bit left to the upside on a seasonal basis for the heating oil and the gasoline has gotten real cheap," O'Grady said.
Even then, others said the heating oil market could only drag crude so far, and it may have met its match at the contract high for now.
"Heating oil is lurking in the background, but I wouldn't buy crude. It's very toppy," another cash trader said.
On the downside, the market focused somewhat on remarks by a top U.N. aide in Geneva Monday highlighting optimism for the implementation soon of the suspended Iraqi oil-for-food deal.
Further, the U.S. government approving another sale from the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve also weighed on prices.
The new measure allows for the sale of $220 million of oil between October 1 and September 30 next year.
